title: How do you read line charts and spot the trends that matter in a case?
description: How to read line charts in case interviews: trends, turning points, growth rates and the dual-axis trap, with a worked example of two companies' sales.
hook: Line charts show change over time, and they are where candidates most often describe instead of think. The goal is to spot the turning point and the gap, and say why they matter.
body:
What to look for

  • Direction: rising, falling, flat.
  • Turning points: when did the trend change, and what happened then?
  • Gaps: between two lines, and whether they are widening.
  • Growth rates: a steeper line is faster growth.

A worked example

Two competitors' sales over five years. Both grew until year three; then the client's line flattens while the rival's keeps rising.

Insight: "The client kept pace until year three, then stalled while the rival kept growing. Something changed in year three: a new product, a price move or a channel. That's what I'd investigate."

The dual-axis trap

When two lines use different axes on the left and right, their crossing point means nothing; the scales are independent. Read each line against its own axis.

Common traps

  • Reading every year's value aloud instead of finding the turning point.
  • Missing that the vertical axis does not start at zero, which exaggerates small changes.
  • Comparing percentages and absolute values on the same chart without noticing.
outro: Next in this topic: How do you read a dense table of numbers quickly in a case interview?
